Why I write

Finance is too important to be left to jargon.

Finance is too important to be left to jargon. Every rate decision, every bond auction, every data centre built with borrowed money ends up in someone's salary, rent or business plan. I write to understand these choices, and to make them understandable.

I write with curiosity, because the most useful question in economics is still why. I write with humility, because markets correct anyone who is too sure of themselves. And I write from Africa as much as from London or New York, because the next chapters of the global economy will not be written only in the old capitals.

This is my notebook: analyses, charts, short notes, and the words of others that shape my thinking. The views are my own. Disagreement is welcome.

About

Mohamed Ramadan

Mohamed Ramadan writes about economics, finance, leadership and artificial intelligence: where capital goes, why it moves, and what it changes for the people and institutions it touches.

He previously served as Chief Financial Officer, and before that as a financial analyst alongside banks and advisory firms. He holds a master's degree in supply chain management from Université Paris-Panthéon-Assas, as well as a master's in finance and accounting and a bachelor's in business administration.

What drives him is curiosity, the habit of asking why a number moved before deciding what it means, and humility, because markets humble everyone and good analysis starts by admitting what we do not know.

UK Autumn Budget 2026

The Boring Budget the Bond Market Ordered

John Healey's first Budget had one real audience: the people who lend Britain money. He gave them exactly what they asked for. The question is what it costs everyone else.

Mohamed Ramadan
28 October 2026 · 6 min readUKDebt & Rates

Key points

  • The OBR puts headroom against the fiscal rules at £15bn in 2029-30, down from £23.6bn in March, rising to £22bn in 2030-31.
  • Gilts barely moved: the 10-year traded at 5.31% in the afternoon, about 20bp below this month's peak, the highest since 2007.
  • The new bank surcharge came in at 3% from January 2027, time-limited to 15 months, against the 8% that had been feared.
  • Growth was nudged up to 1.2% for 2026 but cut to 1% for 2027. The bond market can live with that. Households will feel it.

On Wednesday 28 October 2026, a new Chancellor stood up in the House of Commons and delivered what one fund manager immediately called "the boring Budget that bond markets demanded". He meant it as a compliment. So do I, mostly.

Three weeks earlier, Britain's 30-year gilt had touched about 6.05%, its highest level since 1998. The 10-year had reached its highest since 2007. In that climate, a Chancellor does not have one audience. He has two: the voters in front of him, and the investors who will decide, within minutes, whether his plans are credible. John Healey chose the second audience. That choice tells us more about the state of the British economy than any single measure in the Red Book.

1. The headline number: £15 billion

According to the Office for Budget Responsibility, the government's headroom against its fiscal rules now stands at £15bn in 2029-30. In March, it was £23.6bn. The buffer rises again to £22bn in 2030-31.

Healey was candid about why it shrank. He blamed the conflict in the Middle East for pushing up government borrowing across the G7, and defended using part of the cushion: "That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can."

It is a good line, and a reasonable principle. But notice what it implies. A buffer of £15bn is not large for an economy with debt above 80% of GDP. The OBR itself expects debt-to-GDP at 83.2% this year, rising to 83.8% in 2028-29 before falling to 81.7% by 2032. A few tenths of a point on gilt yields, or one bad year of growth, can consume most of that headroom. The margin of error is small, and everybody in the gilt market knows it.

2. Why the bond market approved

Before the speech, fund managers had said that a buffer below £10bn would disappoint. A Reuters poll had pointed to £10bn to £12bn. Healey delivered £15bn. Gilts rallied in the hours before the Budget and then did almost nothing while he spoke, which is the market's way of saying "priced in". By the afternoon, gilts were outperforming US Treasuries by about five basis points.

The approval came from what was absent. There were no large unfunded giveaways. The new Chancellor inherited one of the tightest fiscal plans in the G10 and chose not to deviate much from it. Borrowing is forecast to fall from 4.2% of GDP at the end of this year to 3.4% next year, and to 1.8% from 2030 to 2032.

In October 2026, the most valuable thing a Chancellor could offer was not a tax cut. It was predictability.

That is the real lesson of this Budget, and it connects directly to what I wrote two weeks ago in The Price of Time. When the cost of money is high, credibility is an asset with a measurable price. Every basis point the gilt market does not add is a saving for the Treasury, for mortgage holders and for every company that borrows against the gilt curve.

3. The banks got off lightly

The most politically charged measure was a new surcharge on bank profits. Reports before the Budget had suggested 8%. The final figure was 3%, applying from January 2027 and ending 15 months later. Bank shares rose before the speech on leaks that the measure would be milder than feared.

I understand the logic. The government needed revenue to fund support for households facing high energy prices, and banks have benefited from higher rates through wider net interest margins. A temporary, modest surcharge raises money without spooking the sector that finances the rest of the economy.

But a 15-month tax on profits tells you something else: the Treasury expects the pressure to be temporary. If rates stay higher for longer, as the Federal Reserve's own projections suggest, that assumption may prove optimistic.

4. Growth: a better year, then a worse one

The OBR raised its forecast for UK growth in 2026 from 1.1% to 1.2%, and Healey cited it as evidence of improvement. In the same document, the OBR cut its forecast for 2027 from 1.6% to 1%.

This matters more than it seems. A budget can be credible on paper and still fragile in practice, because the arithmetic of the fiscal rules depends on growth. A weaker 2027 means lower tax receipts and higher spending on support. If the slowdown is deeper than forecast, the £15bn will not survive contact with reality, and the next Budget will be harder.

5. The long-term move nobody will notice

Buried among the short-term fixes was a decision with very long consequences: the triple lock on the state pension will end from 2030, replaced by a "double lock". The government estimates the saving at about £50bn by 2050.

This is the kind of structural reform that bond markets reward and voters rarely applaud. It does nothing for the next two years. It does a great deal for the debt trajectory of the 2040s. In my view, it is the most serious measure in the Budget, precisely because it is unglamorous.

6. What I would watch next

  1. The gilt remit. Analysts now see the Debt Management Office's issuance plan as the more important event. More Treasury bills and fewer long-dated gilts would support the long end. Heavier long issuance could reverse the calm in a day.
  2. The Bank of England on 5 November. Inflation rose to 3.5% in September. Markets price a near-certain rise in Bank Rate to 4%. Fiscal support for households makes the Bank's job harder, not easier.
  3. Energy prices in January. Suppliers have warned of increases of up to 25%. If they materialise, the political pressure to spend more will return quickly.
  4. Growth in 2027. If the OBR's 1% proves too generous, the buffer goes first.

The verdict

This was not a Budget designed to be loved. It was designed to be believed. In a world where Britain pays more than 5% to borrow for ten years, that is the right priority. A boring Budget is a sign that the Chancellor understood who holds the pen in British fiscal policy today: not the Treasury alone, but the buyers of its debt.

The danger is that "boring" becomes a strategy rather than a starting point. Credibility buys time. It does not buy growth. The next Budget will have to do what this one deliberately avoided: explain how Britain grows its way out of an 83% debt ratio instead of merely managing it.

Sources

  • St. James's Place, "The 2026 Autumn Budget", 28 October 2026
  • Portfolio Adviser, "Treasury's fiscal headroom falls by £8.6bn" and "Gilts steady after budget broadly consistent with market expectations", 28 October 2026

UK Autumn Budget 2026

Breathing Space, at a Price: What Healey's Budget Means for Savers, Founders and Small Firms

Behind the headlines on fiscal headroom, the 2026 Autumn Budget quietly changes the arithmetic for anyone who saves, invests, builds a company or sells online. Here is my reading, line by line.

Mohamed Ramadan
28 October 2026 · 6 min readUKInvesting

Key points

  • The cash ISA allowance stays at £20,000, reversing the planned cut to £12,000, but tax on savings and property income rises by a further two points from April 2027.
  • Founders of high-growth companies will pay 10% capital gains tax on up to £10m of lifetime gains, while Business Asset Disposal Relief is halved to £500,000.
  • 70,000 small businesses will pay no business rates as the threshold rises from £12,000 to £18,000.
  • Online marketplaces will collect VAT at source from sellers with turnover of £90,000 or more, wherever they are based.

Chancellor John Healey described his first Budget as offering millions of people "breathing space". That is a fair description of the intention. But breathing space in a Budget always has a price, and it is usually paid by someone who did not hear their name in the speech.

I read the measures the way a finance director reads a contract: not for what it promises, but for what it changes in the cash flows. Here is what stood out.

1. Savers: one door opens, another narrows

The surprise of the day was a U-turn. In the 2025 Budget, the previous Chancellor had announced that the annual cash ISA allowance would fall from £20,000 to £12,000 for savers under 65. Healey reversed it. Everyone can continue to save up to £20,000 a year in cash ISAs, free of tax.

That is good news for households, and it removes a layer of complexity. But it sits next to a measure that pulls in the opposite direction. From April 2027, tax rates on savings income and property income will rise by a further two percentage points across all bands, on top of the increases already announced last year.

The message is clear: shelter your savings inside an ISA, or pay more. For many families, the practical effect will be a stronger incentive to use the full allowance every year. For landlords and for people with large cash balances outside ISAs, it is a quiet tax rise.

The government also wants to encourage first-time investors through a "Starter ISA". The industry will be consulted, but no date was given. A new first-time buyer ISA will replace the Lifetime ISA from April 2029.

2. Founders: a carrot and a stick

From April 2027, qualifying founders of high-growth, innovative companies will pay a reduced 10% rate of capital gains tax on up to £10m of gains over their lifetime. The detailed rules will follow a consultation.

At the same time, the lifetime limit for Business Asset Disposal Relief, which allows business owners to pay 18% when they sell, will fall from £1m to £500,000 from 6 April 2027.

The government is choosing which entrepreneurs it wants to reward: the ones building scalable, innovative companies, not every owner selling a business.

I think that is a defensible choice, but it will create winners and losers. A technology founder with a fast-growing company gets a generous rate. The owner of a profitable family business who sells after thirty years gets less relief than before. Expect a long argument over the definition of "high-growth" and "innovative" during the consultation.

3. Small businesses: rates relief, paid by gambling

The threshold at which small businesses pay business rates will rise from £12,000 to £18,000 from April. The Chancellor said 70,000 smaller businesses would pay no rates at all, including pubs, village halls and local shops. The cost will be met by higher taxes on gambling and by excluding gambling and vape shops from the rate relief changes.

For a small business, this is real money. Business rates are a fixed cost that does not care whether the month was good or bad. Removing them for the smallest premises improves survival odds at exactly the moment when energy bills are rising again.

4. Online sellers: VAT collected at source

One measure deserves more attention than it received. Online marketplaces will become responsible for collecting VAT at source from sellers on their platforms with a turnover of £90,000 or more, wherever those sellers are based.

This matters well beyond Britain. Many small exporters in Africa and Asia sell to British consumers through large platforms. Until now, VAT compliance for overseas sellers has been uneven. From now on, the platform will collect it. That levels the field for British retailers, and it means that overseas sellers who were under-pricing because they were not paying VAT will see their margins squeezed.

If you run, advise or finance a business that sells into the UK online, this is the measure to model first.

5. Households: small fixes for a big problem

The package for households is a collection of small, targeted measures rather than one big giveaway:

  • The daily standing charge on gas bills, currently about £108 a year, will be removed. Estimates suggest three in five households will pay less, by about £45 a year on average, while heavy gas users may pay more through higher unit prices.
  • A £100 energy payment will go to households in council tax bands A to D, about 20 million homes, at a cost of roughly £2.6bn.
  • Import tariffs will be removed on more than 100 food products, worth an estimated £21 a year per household.
  • The 5p cut in fuel duty is extended until July.
  • The National Living Wage rises by about 3.9% from April 2027, from £12.71 to £13.21 an hour.

None of these will change a family's life. Together, they soften a winter in which energy suppliers have warned that bills could rise by up to 25% in January. The honest description is not "breathing space" but "a smaller squeeze".

6. AI: a small cheque with a large signal

The government will provide £500m for AI security, alongside a new data centre covenant. In the context of what American companies are spending, £500m is modest. But the direction is telling: Britain is positioning itself as a place where AI can be built and secured, not only consumed. The data centre covenant will matter more than the cheque if it makes grid connections and planning faster.

What I would do this week

  1. Use the ISA allowance in full. With savings tax rising in 2027, the value of the wrapper has gone up.
  2. If you are a founder, follow the consultation closely. The definition of a qualifying company will decide who benefits from the 10% rate.
  3. If you plan to sell a business, model the BADR change now. The lower limit applies from 6 April 2027.
  4. If you sell into the UK through a marketplace, re-price for VAT. The platform will collect it whether you are ready or not.
  5. Keep cash for January. Energy costs are the largest risk to household and small-business budgets this winter.

The bottom line

This Budget redistributes rather than transforms. It protects the gilt market's confidence, shifts the burden slightly towards savers, landlords and gamblers, and rewards a particular kind of entrepreneur. For most people, the effects will be small. For the people in the narrow categories it targets, they will be very real.

Sources

  • Portfolio Adviser, Autumn Budget 2026 coverage, 28 October 2026
  • MoneyWeek, Autumn Budget 2026 live coverage

AI

Borrowing for Intelligence: The Debt Behind the AI Build-Out

The companies building artificial intelligence are no longer paying for it from cash alone. They are borrowing on a scale that changes the bond market. That is a financial story before it is a technology story.

Mohamed Ramadan
28 October 2026 · 6 min readAIUnited StatesDebt & Rates

Key points

  • The five largest US hyperscalers issued about $230bn of corporate bonds in the first nine months of 2026, more than double all of 2025, according to research from the Bank of Korea.
  • Goldman Sachs projects hyperscaler capital spending of $600bn to $820bn in 2026, possibly above $1tn in 2027.
  • The core risk is a mismatch: long-dated debt financing assets, such as chips, that may lose value in a few years.
  • For Africa, the lesson is to finance the durable layers of AI, such as energy, connectivity and skills, rather than import the most volatile ones.

For most of the past decade, the largest technology companies were the opposite of borrowers. They generated so much cash that their main financial problem was what to do with it. Buybacks, dividends and acquisitions absorbed the surplus.

That era is ending. In 2026, the companies building artificial intelligence have become some of the largest issuers of corporate debt in the world. I think this is one of the most important financial shifts of the year, and it is still underestimated.

1. The scale

Estimates differ, because definitions differ. Research from the Bank of Korea counts about $230bn of corporate bonds issued by the five largest US hyperscalers in the first nine months of 2026, more than double their total for all of 2025. Broader estimates of AI-related debt this year, including utilities, data centre developers and chipmakers, range from $450bn to well above $500bn.

On the spending side, Goldman Sachs projects hyperscaler capital expenditure of between $600bn and $820bn in 2026, and possibly more than $1tn in 2027. S&P Global Ratings expects roughly $750bn for the five largest companies.

Whatever number you choose, the order of magnitude is the point. We are financing a new industrial base, and a growing share of it is being financed with borrowed money.

2. Why borrow when you are rich?

The obvious question is why companies with enormous cash flows need to borrow at all. There are three answers.

First, the spending has outgrown even their cash generation. Building data centres, buying chips and securing power at this pace absorbs more than operating cash flow can cover without cutting shareholder returns.

Second, debt is cheaper than equity for highly rated companies, even at today's rates. If a company believes the return on an AI data centre will exceed its cost of borrowing, issuing bonds is rational.

Third, borrowing keeps the spending off the income statement for longer. Capital expenditure is depreciated over years. That flatters near-term profits while the build-out continues.

None of this is irrational. But it does change who bears the risk. When an AI investment is financed with retained earnings, a disappointment hurts shareholders. When it is financed with debt, it reaches bondholders, banks, insurers and pension funds.

3. The mismatch that worries me

Here is the part of the story I find most important.

Long-dated debt is being used to finance assets whose economic life may be short.

A 20- or 30-year bond is a promise that the borrower will still be paying in the 2040s and 2050s. The buildings and power connections of a data centre may well last that long. The chips inside them will not. Each generation of AI hardware has made the previous one less competitive within a few years.

If the revenue from AI services grows fast enough, this mismatch does not matter: the cash flows pay for replacement. If revenue grows more slowly than the spending, companies will face a choice between cutting investment and borrowing more. Some credit investors are already demanding higher spreads on project-specific and smaller data centre debt. That is the market doing its job.

4. The utility comparison

In my analysis Intelligence on Tap, I argued that AI is becoming a utility, priced and consumed like electricity. The financing confirms the analogy.

Utilities have always been financed with debt, because their assets are long-lived and their revenues are predictable. The difference is that AI revenues are not yet predictable. We know demand is growing. We do not yet know who will capture the margins: the chip designers, the cloud providers, the model builders, or the companies that use AI to sell something else.

Financing an industry with utility-style debt before it has utility-style revenues is a bet. It may be a good bet. It is still a bet.

5. What it means for markets

  1. More supply of long-dated corporate debt. Large AI issues compete with government bonds for the same investors, at a time when governments are also borrowing heavily. That puts upward pressure on long-term yields.
  2. Concentration risk. A handful of companies now account for a large share of both equity market value and new corporate issuance. A setback for one of them would travel through both markets.
  3. A test for credit discipline. Wider spreads on weaker AI borrowers are healthy. The danger would be if spreads stayed tight because investors assumed the largest names could never disappoint.

6. The lesson for Africa

African governments and companies should watch this closely. The temptation will be to import AI capacity quickly, financed in dollars, because no one wants to be left behind. That would repeat an old mistake: borrowing in foreign currency to buy assets that depreciate fast.

The better strategy is to finance the durable layers of the AI economy: energy generation, transmission, fibre, data centre shells, and above all skills. These assets keep their value across hardware generations. Chips can be leased or bought as services. Power plants and trained engineers cannot be rented from abroad at the moment you need them.

7. Three scenarios for the next five years

It helps to think in scenarios rather than predictions.

The optimistic case. AI revenues grow quickly enough to cover the spending. Enterprises adopt AI services at scale, pricing holds, and the cash flows from data centres repay the debt comfortably. In this world, today's borrowing looks like the early financing of railways or electricity: expensive, but justified.

The middle case. Demand grows, but competition pushes prices down faster than expected. The largest companies remain profitable, but returns on new capacity fall. Weaker borrowers, especially specialised data centre developers and smaller cloud providers, struggle to refinance. Credit spreads widen, some projects are delayed, and the build-out slows without collapsing.

The pessimistic case. A combination of slower adoption, falling prices and higher interest rates leaves too much capacity chasing too little revenue. Asset values fall, lenders take losses, and the companies with the most debt are forced to cut investment sharply. The technology survives. Many of its financiers do not.

I think the middle case is the most likely. It is also the one in which credit analysis matters most, because it separates borrowers who can carry their debt from those who cannot.

8. What I would ask any AI borrower

  1. What is the expected useful life of the assets being financed, and how does it compare with the maturity of the debt?
  2. How much of the revenue is contracted, and for how long?
  3. What happens to cash flow if AI service prices fall by half?
  4. Who bears the risk if a customer walks away: the developer, the lender or the end user?
  5. How much of the spending could be paused without breaching covenants?

The bottom line

Artificial intelligence is being built on borrowed money. That does not make it a bubble. It makes it a credit story, with all the discipline that implies. The investors who will do best are not the ones who believe most strongly in AI. They are the ones who ask, for every dollar lent, how long the asset will last and who will still be paying when it is gone.

  • Goldman Sachs and S&P Global Ratings capex estimates, as reported in October 2026
  • Institute of International Finance, Global Debt Monitor, September 2026

IPOs & Deals

The Record IPO Year That Isn't Quite What It Seems

American IPOs have raised more money in 2026 than in any year in history. Look closer and you find fewer listings, extreme concentration, and a window that is wide open for giants and only half open for everyone else.

Mohamed Ramadan
28 October 2026 · 5 min readIPOs & DealsUnited States

Key points

  • US IPOs raised about $147.6bn through mid-October 2026, more than triple the $44bn raised in all of 2025, according to Renaissance Capital.
  • SpaceX alone raised about $75bn, more than half of the year's total; SK hynix added about $26.5bn.
  • The number of listings is down from last year, even as proceeds hit a record.
  • Anthropic filed for its IPO on 26 October; expectations point to a raise comparable to SpaceX.

Records make good headlines. "Biggest year ever for US IPOs" is true in 2026, and it will be repeated often between now and December. But records can also hide more than they reveal. This one does.

1. The numbers

According to Renaissance Capital, 114 companies had listed in the United States by mid-October, raising $147.6bn. That is more than three times the $44bn raised in the whole of 2025. The previous full-year record, $142.4bn in 2021, was passed in August. The second quarter alone, with 48 listings raising $104.8bn, was the largest quarter ever.

On those figures, the IPO market is booming.

2. The concentration

Now remove two deals. SpaceX raised about $75bn, more than half of the year's total. SK hynix added about $26.5bn. Together, they account for roughly two-thirds of everything raised.

Without its two giants, 2026 would be a good year for IPOs. With them, it is a record. Those are not the same thing.

At the same time, the number of listings is down. Depending on how you count, there have been between a tenth and a third fewer US IPOs than at the same point last year. More money is going to fewer companies.

3. Why the giants are coming now

There are three reasons the largest private companies have chosen 2026 to list.

First, they need capital on a scale that private markets struggle to provide. The companies building rockets, chips and artificial intelligence are spending tens of billions of dollars a year. Public markets remain the deepest pool of equity capital in the world.

Second, their early investors want liquidity. Venture and growth funds that invested five or ten years ago need to return cash to their own investors. A listing is the cleanest way to do it.

Third, valuations are supportive. Investors are willing to pay high multiples for companies associated with AI and frontier technology. When the price is right, founders sell.

The next test is already filed. Anthropic submitted its registration statement on 26 October without disclosing terms. Expectations point to a raise of about $75bn, on a par with SpaceX. If it happens, 2026 will set a record that may stand for a long time.

4. Who is left out

The concentration matters because the IPO market is supposed to do more than finance giants. Historically, it has been the place where medium-sized companies raised growth capital and where ordinary investors could buy into the next generation of businesses early.

That function is weaker than the headline suggests. Mid-sized companies are listing, but in smaller numbers, and investors are more selective. A company without a clear link to AI, defence or energy finds the window narrower than the record implies.

For founders and CFOs, the practical lesson is simple: do not read the market's total as an invitation. Read the deals that look like yours.

5. What it means beyond America

London has spent years trying to win back listings. A record year in New York makes that harder, not easier: the largest companies follow the deepest liquidity, and in 2026 that liquidity is in the United States.

African and Asian companies face the same choice. A listing in New York offers scale and valuation. A listing at home offers proximity to customers and investors who understand the business, and keeps capital markets developing locally. I believe the strongest African exchanges will be built by companies that choose to list at home first and abroad second, not the other way round.

6. The questions I would ask

  1. How much of the money is primary? Capital raised for the company is different from shares sold by existing investors.
  2. What happens after the lock-ups expire? Large insider sales in 2027 could weigh on prices.
  3. How have this year's listings performed? A record that ends with most new shares below their offer price would close the window quickly.
  4. What happens if AI sentiment turns? The year's biggest deals are tied to the same theme. A change of mood would affect all of them at once.

7. Lessons from previous peaks

Record years in equity markets deserve respect and suspicion in equal measure. The two previous peaks in US IPO activity, around 1999-2000 and in 2021, were followed by sharp declines in new listings and in the share prices of many recently listed companies.

That does not mean 2026 will end the same way. The companies listing this year are, on average, much larger and more established than the loss-making start-ups of 2000 or the special purpose acquisition companies of 2021. Many have real revenues and real assets.

But one pattern repeats across cycles: the largest volumes arrive when valuations are highest, because that is when sellers are most willing. Buyers who remember this tend to be more selective at the top of the market, not less.

8. What a founder should do now

If you are a founder or CFO considering a listing in the next two years, the record should change your preparation, not your timetable.

  1. Prepare as if the window will close. Audited accounts, governance and reporting systems take time to build. Having them ready allows you to move when conditions are right rather than when the market is fashionable.
  2. Build a story that does not depend on a theme. If your valuation rests on being "an AI company", it will fall when sentiment turns. If it rests on cash flows, it will hold.
  3. Consider your shareholders after the listing. A company with a small free float and a large lock-up expiry ahead faces volatility it does not control.
  4. Think about where your investors are. A listing close to your customers and your market can build a more loyal shareholder base than a larger but distant exchange.
  5. Keep private options open. Private credit and growth equity remain alternatives for companies that are not ready, or not willing, to accept public-market scrutiny.

The bottom line

2026 is a record year for IPO proceeds and an ordinary year for IPOs. Both statements are true. Understanding the gap between them is the difference between reading markets and reading headlines.

Sources

  • Catenaa, "US IPO Market Hits Record $145.5bn in 2026"

  • StockAnalysis, "All 2026 IPOs"

Why the Bank of England Is About to Raise Rates Again

Inflation is rising, the Budget adds support for households and markets price a hike almost as a certainty. On 5 November, the Bank of England is likely to take Bank Rate to 4%. Here is why, and what it means.

Mohamed Ramadan
28 October 2026 · 5 min readUKDebt & Rates

Key points

  • UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, above expectations, with motor fuels the largest contributor.
  • In September, three of nine Monetary Policy Committee members already voted to raise Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%.
  • On 28 October, market pricing implied a 97% probability of a 25bp rise on 5 November.
  • A hike would be a response to an energy shock, not to an overheating economy, which makes it a delicate decision.

Central bankers dislike surprising markets, and the Bank of England is unlikely to surprise them next week. Almost everything points in one direction: a rise in Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November.

I want to explain why, because the reasons matter more than the decision itself.

1. Inflation has turned up again

Consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in September, from 3.1% in August. It came in above economists' expectations. The largest contribution came from motor fuels, a direct consequence of oil prices pushed higher by the conflict in the Middle East.

This is the problem every central bank fears most: inflation driven by a supply shock. Higher rates cannot produce more oil. They can only reduce demand elsewhere in the economy so that the shock does not spread into wages and prices more broadly.

2. The committee was already moving

In September, the Monetary Policy Committee held Bank Rate at 3.75%, but the vote was six to three. Three members wanted to raise it to 4% immediately. When a third of the committee is already voting to move, and the data then move in their direction, the majority usually follows.

Markets have reached the same conclusion. On 28 October, overnight index swap pricing implied a 97% probability of a 25 basis point rise. A Reuters poll in mid-October found that 54 of 63 economists expected a move to 4% in November. Some banks expect another increase in February 2027.

3. The Budget does not help

Fiscal policy and monetary policy can work together or against each other. This week's Budget leaned, modestly, against the Bank.

Every pound of support for household energy bills is welcome for families. It also keeps demand stronger than it would otherwise be, at a moment when the Bank is trying to cool it.

The support was targeted and the overall package was broadly neutral, which is why the gilt market approved. But the near-term effect is to make the Bank's job slightly harder. Combined with high inflation, it smooths the path to higher rates in the coming months, even though the OBR has cut its growth forecast for 2027 to 1%.

4. The Fed has already moved

The Bank of England does not decide in isolation. In September, the Federal Reserve raised its target range to 3.75%–4%, its first increase since 2023, and most of its policymakers expect to go further. When the world's most important central bank tightens, others face pressure on their currencies and bond markets if they do not.

5. Why this hike is uncomfortable

There is a serious case against moving. Employment has weakened. Growth is forecast to slow sharply next year. Raising rates into a slowdown caused by an external energy shock risks deepening the slowdown without doing much about the cause of inflation.

That is why I expect the Bank to raise rates while sounding cautious, emphasising that future decisions depend on the data. The goal will be to show it takes inflation seriously without committing to a long series of increases.

6. What it means in practice

  1. For households with mortgages: fixed-rate deals already price in higher rates. Anyone coming off a fixed rate in the next year should expect a higher monthly payment than they had planned for in 2024 or 2025.
  2. For savers: deposit rates will drift higher, but the tax changes announced in the Budget will take a larger share of interest income from 2027 outside ISAs.
  3. For companies: the cost of short-term borrowing rises again. Working capital tied up in slow payments becomes more expensive, as I argued in The Price of Time.
  4. For gilts: a hike is priced in. The bigger risk for long-dated bonds is inflation persistence and heavy issuance, not one decision.

What I would tell a CFO this week

  • Assume rates stay higher for longer than your plan from last year.
  • Shorten your cash conversion cycle. Every day of receivables now costs more.
  • Review floating-rate debt and consider fixing part of it while markets are calm.
  • Watch January energy prices: they will shape the Bank's next move more than any speech.

7. Lessons from previous energy shocks

Central banks have faced this dilemma before. In the 1970s, oil price shocks fed into wages and prices for years, partly because central banks were too slow to respond and allowed expectations of inflation to become entrenched. The lesson most policymakers took from that period is that it is dangerous to ignore a supply shock if there is any sign it is spreading into the wider economy.

In 2008 and again in 2011, the European Central Bank raised rates in response to energy-driven inflation, only to reverse course as growth weakened. Those episodes taught the opposite lesson: tightening into a slowdown caused by external factors can make things worse.

The Bank of England's challenge is to steer between these two mistakes. That is why the signals it gives about wages, services inflation and inflation expectations will matter more than the size of any single move.

8. What would change my view

I expect a rise on 5 November, but several developments could change the picture over the coming months:

  1. A sharp fall in oil and gas prices. If the energy shock fades, the case for further increases weakens quickly.
  2. Rising unemployment. A faster deterioration in the labour market would make the committee more cautious.
  3. Services inflation and wage growth. These are the best indicators of whether inflation is becoming entrenched. If they stay contained, the Bank can afford to stop soon.
  4. The gilt market. A disorderly rise in long-term yields would tighten financial conditions on its own and reduce the need for further rate increases.

The bottom line

A rate rise on 5 November would not be a sign that the British economy is overheating. It would be a sign that the Bank of England believes it cannot afford to let a supply shock become a permanent inflation problem. That is a defensive decision, made in difficult conditions, and the cautious tone around it will matter as much as the move itself.

  • Reuters poll of economists, 15 October 2026, as reported by HomeOwners Alliance
  • XTB, UK interest rate forecast 2026–2027

Curiosity and Humility: The Two Disciplines of Good Financial Leadership

Technical skill gets you into finance. It does not keep you right. The leaders I respect most share two habits that no spreadsheet teaches: they keep asking why, and they assume they might be wrong.

Mohamed Ramadan
28 October 2026 · 5 min readLeadership

Key points

  • Curiosity means asking why a number moved before deciding what it means.
  • Humility means designing decisions so that being wrong is survivable.
  • The most expensive mistakes in finance come from confidence, not from ignorance.
  • Both habits can be built deliberately, through questions, rituals and the way teams are organised.

People often ask what makes a good finance leader. The usual answers are technical: accounting, modelling, treasury, negotiation. All of them matter. None of them is enough.

Having worked as a financial analyst and as a Chief Financial Officer, I have come to believe that two habits matter more than any technical skill over a career: curiosity and humility. They sound soft. In practice, they are disciplines, and they decide whether a finance function protects a company or merely reports on it.

1. Curiosity: the habit of asking why

Every finance team produces numbers. Very few interrogate them.

A margin falls by two points. The lazy explanation is "costs went up". The curious question is: which costs, for which products, for which customers, starting when, and why then? Usually the answer is more specific and more useful than anyone expected: a supplier changed terms, a currency moved, a sales team discounted to hit a quarterly target.

A number is not an answer. It is the beginning of a question.

Curiosity is what turns finance from bookkeeping into intelligence. The CFO who understands why the numbers move can warn the chief executive before the problem becomes visible in the accounts. The one who only reports them arrives after the damage is done.

2. Curiosity beyond the company

The same habit applies to the world outside. Interest rates, energy prices, exchange rates and regulation all reach a company's cash flows eventually. A curious finance leader reads widely: central bank minutes, bond market commentary, trade data, the annual reports of competitors and suppliers.

This is not academic. When gilt yields rose sharply in October 2026, the companies that had already shortened their payment cycles and fixed part of their debt were the ones whose leaders had been paying attention months earlier.

3. Humility: designing for being wrong

Humility in finance is not modesty. It is a design principle.

Every forecast is wrong. The only questions are by how much and in which direction. A humble finance leader accepts this and builds decisions that survive error: liquidity buffers, staged investments, options to exit, covenants with room to breathe, scenarios that include outcomes nobody wants to discuss.

Markets punish overconfidence with remarkable consistency. Warren Buffett's line that you only find out who is swimming naked when the tide goes out is really a statement about humility. The people caught out are rarely the ones who lacked information. They are the ones who were too sure.

4. Why confidence is so expensive

The most costly mistakes I have seen in finance did not come from ignorance. They came from confidence:

  • the acquisition that "could not fail" and was paid for with debt that left no margin;
  • the currency exposure left unhedged because "the rate has been stable for years";
  • the project approved because the most senior person in the room wanted it, and no one challenged the assumptions.

In each case, the information to avoid the mistake existed. What was missing was the willingness to say "I might be wrong" early enough to change course.

5. How to build both habits

Curiosity and humility can be practised. Here is what I have found works.

  1. Ask "why" three times. For every significant variance, push past the first explanation. The real cause is usually two or three questions down.
  2. Write down the assumptions. Every forecast should list the three assumptions that matter most and what would prove them wrong.
  3. Hold a pre-mortem. Before a major decision, imagine it has failed a year from now and ask the team to explain why. It surfaces risks that optimism hides.
  4. Reward the messenger. If people are punished for bad news, they will stop bringing it. A finance team's value depends on hearing problems early.
  5. Read outside your field. History, psychology and economics explain behaviour that spreadsheets cannot.
  6. Keep a decision journal. Record why you made a decision and what you expected. Reviewing it later is the fastest way to learn where your judgement is reliable and where it is not.

6. The leader the team needs

Teams take their cues from their leaders. A curious leader creates a team that investigates. A humble leader creates a team that tells the truth. Together, those two qualities produce something every company needs and few have: a finance function that sees problems early and says so clearly.

7. Curiosity and humility in a crisis

These habits are tested most in a crisis, when the pressure to appear certain is greatest.

In a liquidity squeeze, the curious leader asks precise questions immediately: which payments are due this week, which customers are paying late and why, which credit lines can be drawn and on what conditions. The answers turn panic into a plan.

The humble leader, meanwhile, communicates what is known and what is not. Lenders, employees and boards can work with uncertainty. What destroys trust is false confidence that is later contradicted by events. A finance leader who says "here is what we know, here is what we are doing, here is when we will know more" earns the time needed to solve the problem.

8. A note on Africa

I write often about African economies, and these habits matter there in a particular way. Businesses on the continent operate with more volatile currencies, less predictable regulation and thinner capital markets than in London or New York. In that environment, curiosity about the details and humility about forecasts are not refinements. They are survival skills.

The finance leaders I admire most in African companies tend to keep more liquidity than textbooks recommend, hedge more carefully, and question assumptions that would be taken for granted elsewhere. They are not pessimists. They are realists who have learned that the unexpected is normal.

The bottom line

Technical skill makes you useful. Curiosity makes you insightful. Humility keeps you solvent. In a world of higher rates, faster technology and more frequent shocks, the last two are no longer optional. They are the job.

Leadership

Why Smart Organisations Make Bad Decisions

Most bad decisions in companies are not made by foolish people. They are made by capable people inside structures that reward the wrong behaviour. Fix the structure and the decisions improve.

Mohamed Ramadan
28 October 2026 · 5 min readLeadershipOrganisations

Key points

  • Incentives shape decisions more than intelligence does.
  • Information gets filtered as it travels up a hierarchy, so leaders often decide on a cleaner story than reality.
  • Sunk costs and groupthink keep failing projects alive long after the evidence has turned.
  • Good organisations design for dissent, small bets and honest feedback.

When a company makes a bad decision, the first instinct is to look for the person responsible. Sometimes there is one. More often, the decision was made by intelligent, well-meaning people who were doing exactly what the organisation rewarded them for.

I have come to believe that the quality of a company's decisions depends less on the intelligence of its people than on the design of the organisation around them. Here are the four mechanisms I see most often.

1. Incentives beat intentions

People respond to what they are measured and paid on. If a sales team is rewarded on revenue, it will sell at discounts that destroy margin. If a project manager is rewarded for delivering on time, problems will be hidden until the deadline. If a lending officer is rewarded on volume, credit quality will drift.

None of this requires bad intentions. It only requires people to behave rationally inside the system they work in.

Show me the incentive and I will show you the decision.

The first question to ask after a poor decision is not "who made it?" but "what was this person rewarded for?" The answer usually explains more than any analysis of their judgement.

2. Information is filtered on the way up

In any hierarchy, information is summarised as it travels upward. Each layer simplifies, removes uncertainty and, consciously or not, presents the story in a way that reflects well on itself. By the time a problem reaches the board, it may look smaller, later and more manageable than it really is.

Peter Drucker observed that the most important thing in communication is hearing what isn't said. In organisations, what isn't said is usually the bad news.

Leaders who want the truth have to go and get it: visiting operations, talking to people several levels down, reading raw data rather than only polished summaries, and making it safe for people to say "this is not working".

3. Sunk costs keep bad projects alive

Once a company has spent heavily on a project, abandoning it feels like admitting failure. So the project continues, consuming more money, because stopping would make the earlier spending look wasted.

Economically, money already spent is irrelevant to the decision. Only future costs and future benefits matter. Psychologically, it is the most powerful force in the room. The executive who launched the project has a reputation at stake. The team has careers at stake. The board does not want to write off an investment it approved.

The best protection is to agree, before a project starts, on the evidence that would lead to stopping it. When that evidence appears, the decision has already been made in calmer conditions.

4. Groupthink feels like alignment

Teams that work well together develop shared assumptions. That is useful until it isn't. When everyone in the room thinks the same way, nobody tests the assumptions, and dissent starts to feel disloyal.

The psychologist Irving Janis called this groupthink. Its symptoms are familiar: an illusion of invulnerability, pressure on dissenters, self-censorship and the belief that silence means agreement. Some of the most expensive corporate and financial failures in history were approved by unanimous committees.

5. How good organisations decide better

None of these problems can be eliminated. They can be managed. The organisations that decide well tend to share a few practices.

  1. Align incentives with long-term outcomes. Reward margin, not only revenue. Reward quality, not only speed. Defer part of bonuses until results are proven.
  2. Make dissent a role. Assign someone to argue the opposite case before major decisions. It removes the social cost of disagreeing.
  3. Decide on stopping rules in advance. Every major project should have clear milestones and conditions under which it ends.
  4. Make small bets first. Test an idea cheaply before committing heavily. Learning early is much cheaper than learning late.
  5. Shorten the distance between leaders and reality. Fewer layers, direct contact with operations and access to raw data.
  6. Review decisions, not just results. A good decision can produce a bad outcome through bad luck, and vice versa. Learning comes from examining the reasoning, not only the result.

6. The role of the finance function

Finance has a particular responsibility here. It sees the numbers across the organisation, it is less attached to any single project and it can ask uncomfortable questions in a neutral language. A finance team that only reports results is wasting that position. One that challenges assumptions, tracks projects against their original business cases and makes sunk costs visible can improve the quality of every major decision.

7. A short case study

Consider a familiar pattern. A company launches an ambitious new product. Early sales are disappointing, but the team responsible explains that customers need time and that the next version will fix the problems. The executive sponsor, who championed the launch, agrees. The board, which approved the investment, is reassured.

A year later, sales are still weak. More money has been spent on marketing and development. The original business case is no longer mentioned. Eventually, a new chief executive closes the product and writes off the investment.

Every mechanism described above was at work. Incentives rewarded the team for continuing rather than stopping. Information reaching the board was optimistic. Sunk costs made each additional investment feel justified. And nobody in the room wanted to be the first to say it was not working.

A clear stopping rule, agreed at the launch, would have saved most of the money.

8. Decisions in financial institutions

Banks and investment firms are particularly exposed to these mechanisms, because their decisions involve risk that only becomes visible later. A loan that looks profitable today may become a loss in three years. A trading strategy that works in calm markets may fail in a crisis.

That is why the best financial institutions invest heavily in independent risk functions, separate the people who take risks from the people who measure them, and pay part of bonuses in deferred form. These are not bureaucratic burdens. They are organisational designs that counter the natural tendency of capable people to underestimate risks they are rewarded for taking.

The bottom line

Smart organisations make bad decisions when their structures reward the wrong things, hide the truth and punish disagreement. The answer is not to hire smarter people. It is to design organisations in which ordinary people, acting rationally, are led towards good decisions.

From Mobile Money to Capital Markets: Africa's Next Financial Leap

Africa leapfrogged landlines and bank branches. The next leap is harder and more important: turning the savings that now move through phones into long-term capital that finances African growth.

Mohamed Ramadan
28 October 2026 · 5 min readAfricaInvesting

Key points

  • Mobile money solved payments for millions of people who never had a bank account. It has not yet solved long-term savings and investment.
  • Sub-Saharan sovereigns raised about $9.3bn in Eurobonds in January to September 2026, but their repayments rise from about $3.5bn in 2026 to $8.6bn in 2028.
  • Borrowing abroad in dollars remains expensive and risky; deeper local capital markets would reduce that dependence.
  • The opportunity is to connect mobile wallets to local bonds, funds and pensions, safely and simply.

When M-Pesa launched in Kenya in 2007, few people outside the continent understood what was happening. Within a few years, millions of people who had never had a bank account were sending money, paying bills and receiving wages through their phones. Africa had skipped the branch network entirely.

That leap was about payments. The next one is about capital, and it matters even more.

1. What mobile money solved, and what it did not

Mobile money solved the problem of moving money cheaply and safely. It brought people into the financial system and made small transactions practical. In many countries, mobile wallets now hold significant balances.

But a wallet is not an investment. Most of the money held in mobile accounts earns little or nothing for its owners, even when the operators themselves earn interest on the balances they place with banks. Meanwhile, African governments and companies borrow abroad, in dollars, at high rates, because local long-term capital is scarce.

Africa has savings. What it lacks are the channels that turn those savings into long-term local investment.

2. The cost of borrowing abroad

The cost of the current model is visible in the bond market. In February 2026, Côte d'Ivoire raised $1.3bn over 15 years at an effective rate of about 5.39% after hedging into euros, a strong result. Others pay far more: DR Congo's debut 10-year bond cost 9.5%, and Kenya refinanced at 10.4% a bond originally issued at 6.9%.

Sub-Saharan sovereigns raised about $9.3bn in Eurobonds between January and September 2026, more than in all of 2025. Their repayments, according to the World Bank, rise from about $3.5bn in 2026 to $8.6bn in 2028. Every dollar of that debt carries currency risk: when the local currency weakens, the burden grows, even if nothing else has changed.

3. The case for local capital markets

Deep local capital markets reduce that vulnerability. When governments and companies can borrow in their own currency from their own citizens and institutions, they are less exposed to swings in global interest rates and exchange rates. Savers earn a return. Capital stays at home.

The building blocks exist in many countries: government securities markets, regional exchanges such as the BRVM in West Africa, growing pension funds and asset managers. What is missing is scale and access. Most ordinary savers cannot easily buy a government bond or a diversified fund.

4. Connecting the wallet to the market

This is where mobile money becomes more than a payment system. The same infrastructure that lets someone send money to a relative could let them buy a small slice of a government bond, contribute to a pension or invest in a regulated fund.

Some countries have already experimented with mobile-distributed government bonds and savings products. The potential is enormous: millions of small savers, each investing modest amounts regularly, can add up to a meaningful pool of local long-term capital.

5. What has to go right

This will not happen automatically. Several conditions matter.

  1. Trust and protection. Savers must be confident that their money is safe. That requires strong regulation, clear disclosure and protection against fraud.
  2. Simplicity. Products must be easy to understand and easy to exit. Complexity is the enemy of inclusion.
  3. Macroeconomic stability. People will not lend to their own government for ten years if inflation erodes the value of their savings. Credible central banks and sound public finances come first.
  4. Interoperability. Wallets, banks, exchanges and custodians must connect smoothly, ideally across borders within regional unions.
  5. Financial education. Investment carries risk. Savers need to understand the difference between a deposit, a bond and a share.

6. Why it matters for growth

Infrastructure, housing, energy and manufacturing all need long-term finance. Today, much of it comes from abroad, in foreign currency, at high cost. If even a fraction of the savings that move through African phones could be channelled into local long-term investment, the cost of capital would fall and the continent would depend less on the mood of global markets.

That is the real meaning of the price of time for Africa. Capital that stays at home, in local currency, is capital that does not need to be repaid at the mercy of the dollar.

7. The role of regional integration

Many African markets are small on their own. A single country's bond or equity market may not have enough issuers or investors to be liquid. Regional integration changes that.

The West African Economic and Monetary Union already shares a currency, a central bank and a regional stock exchange. Central Africa has its own monetary union and is working to integrate its financial markets. The African Continental Free Trade Area aims to reduce barriers to trade across the continent, and financial integration is a natural next step.

For savers, regional markets mean more choice and better diversification. For issuers, they mean a larger pool of investors in a shared currency. Mobile money platforms that operate across borders within these unions could become the distribution channel that makes regional markets accessible to ordinary people.

8. What policymakers and investors can do

  1. Issue more local-currency debt in small denominations, distributed through mobile channels where regulation allows.
  2. Strengthen pension systems, so that a growing share of long-term savings is invested in local assets.
  3. Protect savers first, with clear regulation of digital investment products and enforcement against fraud.
  4. Encourage local listings, so that growing African companies offer citizens a chance to share in their success.
  5. Measure progress honestly, tracking not only the number of accounts opened but the amount of long-term capital mobilised.

The bottom line

Africa's first financial leap connected people to payments. The second must connect their savings to their own economies. It is harder, because it requires trust, stability and good regulation, not just technology. But the reward is a continent that finances more of its own future.

Sources

  • World Bank, Africa's Pulse and debt data on sub-Saharan Eurobond repayments, 2026
  • Bond issuance data for Côte d'Ivoire, DR Congo and Kenya, 2026, as cited in The Price of Time

AI and the CFO: What Changes in the Finance Function

Artificial intelligence will not replace the finance function. It will change what finance is paid for. The work that can be described will be automated. The work that requires judgement will become more valuable.

Mohamed Ramadan
28 October 2026 · 5 min readAILeadership

Key points

  • Tasks that can be described precisely, such as reconciliations, first drafts of reports and routine analysis, will increasingly be done by AI.
  • Judgement, accountability, negotiation and trust will become the core of the finance role.
  • The biggest risk is not job loss but confident errors: AI can produce plausible numbers that are wrong.
  • Finance teams should adopt AI with controls: clear ownership, verification and an audit trail.

Every few years, a technology arrives that is supposed to transform finance. Spreadsheets did. Enterprise software did. Most of the time, the transformation is slower and stranger than predicted. Artificial intelligence is different in one respect: it can do work that previously required a trained person to read, write and reason.

I want to set out, as clearly as I can, what I think changes for finance teams and what does not.

1. What AI already does well

Large language models and related tools are already useful for a wide range of finance tasks:

  • drafting commentary on monthly results from structured data;
  • summarising contracts, loan agreements and board papers;
  • reconciling transactions and flagging anomalies;
  • answering routine questions about policies and procedures;
  • producing first versions of models, memos and presentations.

None of this replaces a finance professional. It removes a large share of the time spent on preparation, so that people can spend more time on interpretation.

The rule I use is simple: if a task can be described precisely, it will increasingly be done by a machine.

2. What becomes more valuable

What remains, and grows in value, is the work that cannot be fully described:

  1. Judgement. Deciding which of several plausible interpretations is right, and what to do about it.
  2. Accountability. Someone must sign the accounts, stand behind the forecast and answer to the board, the auditors and the regulators. A model cannot.
  3. Negotiation. Agreeing terms with lenders, suppliers and investors depends on trust and relationships.
  4. Context. Knowing the history of a business, the people involved and the reasons behind past decisions.
  5. Communication. Explaining numbers to people who are not accountants, in a way that changes their decisions.

A machine can prepare ten financing structures in a minute. Choosing the right one, and convincing a bank and a client to sign it, remains deeply human.

3. The real risk: confident errors

The most important risk is not that AI will take jobs. It is that it will produce answers that look right and are wrong.

AI systems can generate plausible figures, references and explanations that do not match reality. In finance, where a small error in an input can become a large error in a valuation or a covenant calculation, that is dangerous. The danger increases precisely because the output is fluent and confident.

The answer is not to avoid AI. It is to use it with the same controls we apply to any important process.

4. How to adopt AI responsibly

  1. Keep a human owner for every output. Each report or analysis produced with AI should have a named person responsible for checking and approving it.
  2. Verify against source data. Figures must be traceable to the ledger, the contract or the original document.
  3. Protect confidential information. Use tools and settings that keep company data secure and within the right jurisdiction.
  4. Keep an audit trail. Record what was produced by AI, what was changed and who approved it.
  5. Start with low-risk tasks. Drafting and summarising before forecasting and valuation.
  6. Train people. Teams need to understand both what the tools can do and how they fail.

5. The economics of the change

AI also changes the cost structure of finance. In Intelligence on Tap, I argued that intelligence is becoming a utility, billed by consumption. For a finance function, that means a new line in the budget: the cost of tokens and AI services, set against the time saved.

The return will be real but uneven. Teams that redesign their processes around AI will gain the most. Teams that simply add AI to old processes will gain little and may add risk.

6. What it means for careers

For people starting in finance, the traditional apprenticeship of reconciliations, data gathering and first drafts will shrink. That is a challenge, because those tasks were how many of us learned the business. Organisations will need to find new ways to build judgement in junior staff: more exposure to real decisions, more mentoring and more explanation of why, not just what.

For experienced professionals, the opportunity is to spend more time on the parts of the job that matter most. The finance leader of the next decade will manage a team of people and machines, and will be judged on the quality of the decisions that team supports.

7. A practical roadmap for a finance team

For a finance team starting with AI, I would suggest a staged approach over twelve to eighteen months.

First, map the work. List the recurring tasks of the team and estimate the time each takes. Identify those that are repetitive, rule-based and low-risk.

Second, run small pilots. Choose two or three tasks, such as drafting monthly commentary or summarising contracts, and test AI tools with clear success measures: time saved, error rates and user satisfaction.

Third, build controls before scaling. Define who checks outputs, how sources are verified and how data is protected. Involve internal audit early.

Fourth, redesign processes. Once tools are proven, change the process itself rather than adding AI to the old one. A monthly close redesigned around automated reconciliation and drafting can be shorter and more reliable.

Fifth, invest in people. Use the time saved to develop analysis, business partnering and communication skills across the team.

8. The questions boards should ask

  1. Where is AI already being used in our finance function, and who approved it?
  2. How do we verify the accuracy of AI-assisted reports and forecasts?
  3. What data are we sharing with external AI providers, and under what terms?
  4. How are we developing the judgement of junior staff if routine tasks are automated?
  5. What is the measurable return on our AI spending so far?

The bottom line

AI will not end the finance function. It will change what finance is paid for. Preparation becomes cheap. Judgement, accountability and trust become the job. The finance teams that understand this early will be more valuable than ever.

The Price of Time: Britain's 6% Gilt Has Just Ended the Era of Free Slow Money

A 6% gilt marks the end of an era in which slow, opaque money was free. The winners of the next decade will be those who make time cheap again.

Mohamed Ramadan
15 October 2026 · 7 min readUKDebt & RatesAfrica

Key points

  • On 1 October 2026, the yield on Britain's 30-year gilt touched 6.03%, a level last seen in January 1998.
  • Every 0.25 point on gilt yields adds roughly £2.5 billion a year to UK debt interest.
  • £1 million stuck for three days now costs about £308 in lost interest, against £8 in 2021.
  • Sending $200 to sub-Saharan Africa costs 8.46% on average, against 6.36% worldwide.

On the morning of 1 October 2026, the yield on Britain’s 30-year government bond touched 6.03%. The last time London paid that much to borrow for a generation was January 1998, a year after the Bank of England was handed the keys to interest rates and a year before the euro was born.

Most commentary will treat this as a British story: a new Chancellor, a Budget on 28 October, a nervous bond market. I want to argue something different, and more uncomfortable.

My thesis is simple: a 6% gilt marks the end of an era in which slow, opaque money was free. For fifteen years, near-zero rates hid the true cost of the way money moves between Britain and Africa. That subsidy is gone. Every day a payment waits, every pound that sits idle, every point of spread on a transfer is now a measurable loss, and Africa pays the largest share of it. The winners of the next decade will not be those with the cleverest token, but those who make time cheap again.

Here is the case.

1. The staircase, not the spike

Markets like to call every bad day a “spike”. But look at the sequence. The 30-year gilt went above 5% during the 2022 mini-budget crisis, then to 5.69% in September 2025, to 5.78% in May 2026, to about 5.9% in September, and to 6.03% on 1 October. The 10-year reached 5.51%, its highest since July 2007.

When a spike repeats itself four times in four years, it is not a spike. It is a staircase, and staircases are built on foundations:

  • Energy and war. With the Strait of Hormuz still disrupted and oil back above $100 a barrel, UK inflation has turned up again: 3.1% in August, with the Bank of England itself projecting about 3.75% by year-end and slightly above 4% in early 2027.
  • Washington moved first. The Federal Reserve raised rates to 3.75–4% on 16 September, its first hike since 2023, and most of its policymakers expect more.
  • London’s own arithmetic. The Bank held at 3.75%, but three of its nine policymakers already voted to raise. The Treasury must still sell about £246 billion of gilts this fiscal year.

The point is not that rates are high. It is that nobody serious expects them to return to zero. The Fed’s own projections push the first cuts out to 2028. That changes the economics of everything that is slow.

2. When the bond market writes the Budget, it writes everyone’s budget

In 1993, James Carville, Bill Clinton’s strategist, said that if he were reincarnated he would want to come back as the bond market, because “you can intimidate everybody”. African finance ministers have lived with that intimidation for decades, sitting in London roadshows being told that their spreads reflect their “credibility”.

This autumn, the lecture is being delivered to a G7 Treasury. In March, the Office for Budget Responsibility gave the Chancellor about £23.6 billion of headroom against the fiscal rules. Higher yields have since cut it to an estimated £8.5–16 billion. Every 0.25 point on gilt yields adds roughly £2.5 billion a year to debt interest.

Why should an importer in Douala or a treasurer in Lagos care? Because the gilt and the Treasury bill are the benchmarks against which their own money is priced. Sub-Saharan sovereigns raised about $9.3 billion in Eurobonds between January and September 2026, more than in all of 2025, and their repayments rise from about $3.5 billion in 2026 to $8.6 billion in 2028, according to the World Bank. When the base rate of the world rises, Africa’s bill rises with it, even if nothing in Africa has changed.

3. The hierarchy is blurring at the top, not at the bottom

Here is a comparison nobody in the City will put on a slide. In February 2026, Côte d’Ivoire raised $1.3 billion over 15 years, nearly five times oversubscribed, at an effective 5.39% after hedging into euros. On 1 October, Britain paid 5.51% for 10 years and 6.03% for 30 years in its own currency.

The comparison is imperfect: currencies, maturities and dates differ, and the chart says so. But the order of magnitude makes the argument. The old hierarchy, in which the North borrows cheaply and the South pays for its sins, is blurring at the top. It is not blurring at the bottom: DR Congo’s debut 10-year bond cost 9.5%, and Kenya refinanced at 10.4% a bond originally issued at 6.9%.

This matters for my thesis. If even London now pays for time, then the price of time is no longer a “risk premium” that Africa alone carries. It is a global cost of capital, and the question becomes: who wastes it, and who saves it?

4. The hidden tax: what slow payments really cost

This is where the argument becomes concrete.

Benjamin Franklin wrote in 1748 that “time is money”. For most of the past fifteen years, it wasn’t. With Bank Rate at 0.10% in 2021, £1 million stuck for three days in a correspondent banking chain cost about £8 in lost interest. Nobody noticed, so nobody fixed it.

At today’s 3.75%, the same three days cost about £308. At the 10-year gilt rate, about £453. Same delay, 37 times more expensive.

Now multiply. Every supplier invoice paid from Africa via London. Every payroll. Every FX conversion done on an “indicative” rate that moves before the money lands. Every balance left idle in a non-interest account “just in case”. In a zero-rate world, these were inconveniences. In a 6% world, they are a hidden tax, and the slowest rail pays it.

5. Africa pays the highest toll to receive its own money

The World Bank’s latest data are unambiguous. Sending $200 to sub-Saharan Africa costs 8.46% on average, against 6.36% worldwide, 4.59% through digital channels and 14.99% through a bank. The UN target is 3% by 2030.

High rates make this worse, not better. When money is expensive, every intermediary in the chain has an incentive to hold funds a little longer and to price risk a little higher. Africa does not only pay more to borrow. It pays more to receive.

6. Objections, and why they don’t hold

“Rates will fall again, so this will pass.” Perhaps, eventually. But the Fed does not expect cuts before 2028, and the Bank of England projects inflation above 4% in early 2027. More importantly, a business model that only works at zero rates is not a business model. It is a bet.

“Stablecoins will fix it.” They will help, and London is serious about them. In June 2026, the Bank of England finalised its regime for systemic sterling stablecoins: up to 70% of reserves in UK government debt maturing within six months, the rest at the Bank, and a cap of £40 billion per coin. The FCA regime enters into force on 25 October 2027.

But read the design carefully. A coin at the cap could hold £28 billion of short-dated gilts. London has created a new buyer for its own debt, at the short end, while the pain sits at thirty years. The regime is built first to make sterling tokens safe and to fund the state, not to solve the last mile into Douala, Accra or Lagos. A token settles in minutes. Converting it into CFA francs or naira at a fair rate, with compliance, liquidity and a bank account at the other end, still does not. The bottleneck is not the technology. It is liquidity, trust and the last mile.

“This is a British problem.” Section 2 answers it: the benchmark channel carries London’s price of time straight into every African balance sheet.

The real price of a cross-border payment is not the rate. It is the rate multiplied by the time.

7. What I would tell an African CFO this week

  1. Stop holding idle sterling. Cash waiting for an invoice in a non-interest account is now a real loss.
  2. Measure your payment cycle in days, then in pounds. Every day saved in settlement is margin.
  3. Lock rates when markets are open. In a volatile month, the gap between a firm quote and an indicative one can be your profit.
  4. Watch 28 October and 5 November. The Budget, then the Bank of England’s next decision. A hike strengthens the case for converting early rather than late.
  5. Refinance before you have to. The window is open, but narrower than it looks.

The bond market has no ideology. It does not care about Westminster or Yaoundé, about speeches or slogans. It asks one question of everyone: what is your time worth?

For fifteen years, the answer was “almost nothing”, and the world built its payment systems around that illusion. In October 2026, London’s answer is 6%. Those who understand what that means will spend the next decade making time cheap again. The others will keep paying for it, three days at a time.
